Cricket spread all over India because of a series of victories that made the game hugely popular. In 1983 the Indian team won the World Cup for cricket under the captainship of Kapil Dev, and this was a historic victory that instantly won cricket great popularity across the country. In the same year Sunil Gavaskar broke the earlier record of the maximum number of centuries in test cricket. In 1985 India won the 'Benson and Hedges' World Championship of cricket. As a result cricket came to be played in all States to a lesser or greater extent, though this happened at the cost of indigenous Indian games. A few movies were also produced around the theme of cricket, and live telecasts of the full five days or of one day of the matches became available, which carried the game to people everywhere.

The economy of movies is changing because the way movies are shown and earned from has changed completely. The concept of one screen and one cinema hall has given way to multiplexes, and the days of a movie running for 100 weeks in one cinema hall are over. Now one movie runs in thousands of cinema halls in India and abroad at the same time, and Hindi movies compete with 'global' movies as they have reached every nook and corner of the world. Because of this, the production of movies has attained the status of an industry that employs crores of people. The movie industry in regional languages is also thriving.

India has many official languages such as Hindi, Marathi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Urdu and others, and each of these Indian languages also has its own dialects. The number of these dialects is now on the decline. Timely steps should be taken to nurture them, because if they disappear we will lose an important part of our heritage. A dialect carries the way of speaking, and therefore the life and identity, of the people of a particular region, so losing it means losing that part of our past. The list of the languages of Nagaland in 1961 shows how great this variety can be, and because of it the Kohima radio station had to make its broadcasts in 25 languages, which included English, Hindi, Naga dialects and 16 Naga languages. There is also a new pressure on this variety. Due to the process of globalisation which began after 1990, the English language has been gaining ground in India and is becoming the language of livelihood, as it opens the doors to multiple job opportunities. It is necessary to ensure that this process does not endanger the very existence of regional languages. Keeping the dialects alive is therefore the way to protect both our heritage and our regional languages.

The changing lifestyle has had its effect on newspapers, and newspapers in turn have influenced individual as well as community life. During the early post-independence period newspapers had multiple objectives. They were expected not only to give the news of daily events, but also to give impetus to industry and commerce by printing advertisements. They worked to shape public opinion, to direct it towards constructive work and at times to lead it, to carry on the task of public education and to keep a watch over the government machinery. Earlier newspapers were black and white, but with the changing times colour printing became common. Earlier a newspaper was thought to be the mouthpiece of its taluka or district, but now newspapers have to face tough competition from the State level newspaper chains. On the whole newspapers are now becoming more active and their scope has enlarged. They now raise funds for drought affected and flood affected people, help meritorious students from lower income groups to go for higher education, and organise or sponsor cultural programmes. In this way newspapers have become an inseparable part of our lives.

Television came to India during the post-independence period. Earlier it was black and white and now it is coloured. In the beginning it was limited to some selected programmes and fixed time-slots, but gradually its scope was enlarged to include educational programmes, news bulletins and detailed reporting of the tours of the President and the Prime Minister. During the telecast of Ramayana and Mahabharat a majority of the people used to sit glued to the television set, and these serials proved the popularity of this medium. Then in 1991 the CNN channel showed to the entire world a live visual reporting of the Iraq war, and at this stage the world of Indian news channels changed completely. In 1998 STAR (Satellite Television Asia Region), a private media house, entered India, and the uninteresting, monotonous and propagandist news telecasts of the early period underwent a sea change. The language, the technique of presentation, studios equipped with the latest technology and the use of OB (outdoor broadcasting) vans have expanded the scope of Indian T.V. channels still further and brought in transparency and variety. Now every nook and corner of the country is connected, and this has had a great impact on politics.
